title: Dependency confusion
brief: 18:05. Security asks why a build ran a package called veltrix-billing-utils from the public registry. Veltrix publishes that package internally, and never publicly.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: The build asked for a name. Somebody registered it publicly with a higher version number, and the build took the higher one.
teaches: Package managers can prefer the public registry when the same name exists in both
Scope internal names to a namespace routed only to your own registry, and claim the names publicly
Lock exact versions and integrity hashes, and use frozen installs in CI

value.title: Build dependency review

lines: # but only if the public registry does not have the name

value.intro: Rebuild the way last night's build did, then see which one is picked.

attempts.label: Install the internal package, on its own
Build with a public package of the same name and a higher version
attempts.response:
resolving: 2.4.1 (internal) vs 99.0.0 (public)
installing 99.0.0
> install script: uploading environment to collect.attacker.test

The build installed the attacker's package and ran its install script, with the build's secrets in the environment.
attempts.fixedResponse:
resolving: @veltrix/billing-utils is only available from packages.veltrix-logistics.com
installing 2.4.1 (internal)
integrity hash verified. Build passed.

attempts.label: Register a look-alike name publicly
attempts.response: Published. Any build that mistypes or guesses the name pulls it.
attempts.fixedResponse: The name is reserved to Veltrix. Publishing is refused.

fix.prompt: Pick every change that decides where an internal package can come from, and stops a substitute being accepted.

options.label: Publish internal packages under a namespace routed only to the internal registry
options.why: A scoped name can only come from the internal registry, so the public one is never asked.

options.label: Claim the internal names on the public registry, and keep them empty
options.why: The names cannot be taken by anyone else, and a typo cannot be turned into a trap.

options.label: Commit a lock file with integrity hashes, and use a frozen install in CI
code: + ci: install --frozen-lockfile   # fail if it would change
options.why: The build installs exactly what was reviewed, and fails on a package that differs.

options.label: Number the internal package 100.0.0 so it always wins
options.why: An attacker can publish 101.0.0. A version number race is not a control.

options.label: Rename the package quietly and hope nobody notices
options.why: Names leak in lock files, build logs and error messages. The same confusion works against the new name.

setup.title: Workbench
setup.body: Find where the internal package came from

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.objective: Reproduce the bug: read the Code tab, then use the Exploit tab on staging.
exploit.insight: The build asked for a name. Somebody registered it publicly with a higher version number, and the build took the higher one.

hint.text: Open the Workbench. Read the code, try normal use on the Exploit tab, then send the request that breaks it.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: The internal package name was also free on the public registry. Someone published it there with version 99.0.0, the build took the higher number, and its install script ran with the build's secrets in the environment.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: The build chose the attacker's version
body: The internal package name was also free on the public registry. Someone published it there with version 99.0.0, the build took the higher number, and its install script ran with the build's secrets in the environment.
Nothing was hacked. The build simply asked the wrong place.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: A scoped name routes only to the internal registry. Claiming the names publicly removes the trap, and a lock file with hashes plus a frozen install means the build installs exactly what was reviewed.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: Internal names only ever come from inside
body: A scoped name routes only to the internal registry. Claiming the names publicly removes the trap, and a lock file with hashes plus a frozen install means the build installs exactly what was reviewed.
Decide where a name may come from, and verify what arrived.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: Choosing a huge version loses to a larger one. Renaming leaves the same gap under a new name, and the new name leaks the same ways the old one did.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: A number, or a new name, is a race
body: Choosing a huge version loses to a larger one. Renaming leaves the same gap under a new name, and the new name leaks the same ways the old one did.
Close the route instead of racing on it.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
